newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SOUTHERN AFRICA SEEN AS AFRICAN INTEGRATION MODEL.
newsitem.headline: SOUTHERN AFRICA SEEN AS AFRICAN INTEGRATION MODEL.

text.p: Southern Africa's willingness to press ahead with economic development was a model for reaching African economic integration, African Development Bank president Ommar Kabbaj said on Thursday.
He told reporters in Johannesburg he had admired how seriously leaders addressed economic matters at a recent summit of the 12-member Southern African Development Community (SADC).
"I was much impressed with the seriousness with which the leaders of SADC deal with their economic problems and in our views at the bank, SADC is really going to be the model for African integration.
"There is no other region presently which presents the same opportunities, the same willingness, the same readiness to go ahead with economic development" Kabbaj said.
"This is going to be the region that will be the model for the African common market or African unity."

He said the regional economic giant South Africa, which joined the bank in December 1995, played a major role in SADC, which includes Namibia, Lesotho, Swaziland, Botswana, Malawi, Mozambique, Angola, Tanzania, Zambia, Zimbabwe and Mauritius.

"Everybody welcomed South African membership because it made the bank truly continental," he said, but added the bank's leadership was disappointed when South Africa only took a one percent stake in the development bank.
"In the future if South Africa wishes to enlarge its shareholding, I'm sure that the membership at large will accomodate its request," he said.
"We will have in the near future a general capital increase or a selective capital increase...this would be perhaps an occasion for South Africa to adjust its share in the bank."
The African Development Bank was founded in 1964 and has a capital base of around $24 billion. It has 77 members, 24 of them outside Africa.
In July, African members of the bank put off until May 1997 a decision on giving donor nations a greater shareholding in return for increased funding.
The 24 non-African donor members agreed at their annual meeting in May to a three-year replenishment for the ADB's soft loans arm -- the African Development Fund -- worth $2.6 billion.
Kabbaj said the bank had about $3 billion in the fund at present.
Kabbaj said on Thursday that South Africa was the only African country to have agreed to contribute to the fund, the sole source of funds for three quarters of the bank's members.
"South Africa has not announced a figure yet, they are in the process of having this approved by the government and going through the necessary legal requirements.
"But politically, South Africa is showing its solidarity with the poorest countries...of Africa, most of them are the poorest in the world".
